intro: This unit is about how the Talmud is studied, and what it teaches about being kind. You will see two people share one page. They read out loud. They ask questions. They disagree, and they stay friends.

Then you will read seven kindness rules the rabbis wrote down. Visiting the sick. Welcoming a guest. Honoring parents. Not shaming anyone. Bringing back lost things. Giving a share. Feeding animals first.
By the end, you will be able to study with a partner the way the rabbis did. And you will be able to say who each kindness rule helps.
bigQuestion: How do people learn the Talmud together, and who do its kindness rules help?

timeline.t: Find a partner. In Jewish tradition, a study partner is called a chavruta.
Open one page between you. Sit close. Both of you look at the same line.
Read a line out loud. Then let your partner read the next one.
Stuck on a word? Ask. Hillel said a shy person cannot learn.
Disagree? Say why, and say it gently. Point to the page.
Remember the two houses. They argued for years and still stayed one family.
Read a kindness rule from the rabbis, like visiting the sick.
Say who the rule helps. The guest, the parent, the owner, the animal.
Try one rule this week. Then tell your partner how it went.

words.d: a study partner; two people who read the Talmud together and ask each other questions
a house of study, a room where people learn Talmud, often in pairs and out loud
a short book of rabbis' sayings inside the Mishnah; the name means chapters of the fathers
the students who followed Hillel's way of reading the rules
a rule in the Torah; the rabbis also use it for a good deed; more than one is mitzvot
to make someone feel small in front of others; the rabbis said never to do it
a secret detail that shows a lost thing is really yours
giving a share to people who need it; the word comes from a word for fair

test.why: A chavruta is a study partner. The word comes from a word for friend.

test.q: How did the rabbis study the Talmud?
choices: Out loud, in pairs, with questions
test.why: Jewish tradition studies the Talmud out loud with a partner, asking questions.

test.q: Who said to get yourself a teacher and a friend?
test.why: The saying is Joshua ben Perachyah's, in Pirkei Avot 1:6.

test.q: What did the Talmud's voice call both houses' words?
test.why: Eruvin 13b says these and those are the words of the living God.

test.q: Why does the Talmud say the rule follows Hillel's house?
choices: They were gentle and taught the other side first
test.why: The Talmud says Hillel's students were gentle and taught Shammai's view before their own.
A mitzvah is a rule in the Torah. The rabbis also use it for a good deed.

test.q: Who ran to welcome three strangers?
test.why: Genesis 18 says Abraham ran to the strangers and fed them.

test.q: What does the owner of a lost thing give the finder?
test.why: The Mishnah in Bava Metzia says the owner gives a sign, a secret detail.

choices: Giving a share to people in need
test.why: Tzedakah is giving a share to people who need it. The word comes from a word for fair.

test.q: When does the Talmud say to feed your animals?
test.why: Berakhot 40a says to feed your animals before you sit down to eat.

write.prompt: Pick one kindness rule from this unit. Tell what the Torah or the Talmud says about it. Name where it comes from, like Genesis 18 or Bava Metzia. Then say who the rule helps and how you could do it.
tips: Name the book or tractate you are talking about.
Say "the rabbis said" or "the Torah says" when you tell what it teaches.
Use a word from this unit, like mitzvah or chavruta.
Tell who the rule helps, and one thing you could do.

title: Learning Together

chapters.title: Two Voices, One Page
chapters.bigQuestion: Why do people study the Talmud with a partner, out loud, instead of alone and quiet?

story.title: Stuck on the Same Word
story.kicker: Two kids share one big page, and one word stops them both.
paragraphs: Maya and Leo sit at one desk. One big book is open between them. It is a page of the Talmud. The words are small. Some are Hebrew. Some are Aramaic, an old language. Their teacher says, "Read it together. Out loud."

Maya reads a line. Leo reads the next line. Then they both stop. There is a word they do not know. Maya says, "I think it means a lamp." Leo says, "I think it means a door." They look at each other. They are stuck on the same word.
Maya does not get mad. She says, "Show me why you think door." Leo points to the line above. It talks about a house. Maya nods. Then she points to the line below. It talks about light. Leo nods too.

Their teacher walks by. "Good," she says. "That is how the rabbis did it. Two people. One page. Lots of questions." Maya and Leo laugh. They still do not know the word. But they know more than they did.
story.think: Maya and Leo did not agree. What did they do instead of fighting? Why did that help?

lessons.title: What a Chavruta Is
lessons.mainIdea: Jewish tradition studies the Talmud in pairs, out loud, with questions.
reading: The Talmud is not read alone in a quiet corner. It is studied with a partner. The word for a study partner is *chavruta*. It comes from a word that means friend.
Two partners sit at one page. One reads. The other listens. Then they trade. They ask each other, "What does this mean?" They talk out loud. The room gets noisy.
A room for this kind of study has a name. It is a beit midrash. That means house of study. Jews have studied this way for a very long time.

words.d: a study partner; two people who read the Talmud together and ask each other questions
a house of study, a room where people learn Talmud, often in pairs and out loud

look.title: Picture the Room
look.text: Look at a long room with long tables. At every table, two people sit close. One big book is open between them. One person points at a line. The other shakes her head and points at a different line. Everyone is talking. Nobody is shouting. It is loud, but it is happy.
look.prompt: What do you see the partners doing? Why do you think they sit two by two?

check.q: What is a chavruta?
check.why: A chavruta is a study partner. The word comes from a word for friend.

check.q: How do partners study the Talmud?
check.why: Partners read out loud and ask each other questions. The room is noisy.

check.q: What is a beit midrash?
check.why: Beit midrash means house of study. People learn there, often in pairs.

lessons.title: Get Yourself a Friend
lessons.mainIdea: Pirkei Avot says: find a teacher, and get yourself a friend to study with.
reading: There is a small book inside the Mishnah. It is called *Pirkei Avot*. That means chapters of the fathers. It is full of short sayings by rabbis.
One saying comes from a rabbi named Joshua ben Perachyah. He lived about 2,100 years ago. He said: get yourself a teacher. And get yourself a friend to learn with.
Jewish tradition reads this as a rule for study. A teacher shows you the way. A friend walks it with you. That friend is your chavruta.

words.d: a short book of rabbis' sayings inside the Mishnah; the name means chapters of the fathers

look.title: A Saying to Remember
look.text: Joshua ben Perachyah said: Make yourself a teacher, get yourself a friend to study with, and judge every person on the good side.
look.cite: Mishnah Avot 1:6, retold in simple words; compare Charles Taylor, Sayings of the Jewish Fathers, 1877
look.prompt: The saying has three parts. Say them in your own words. Which one is about a chavruta?

check.q: What does Pirkei Avot mean?
check.why: Pirkei Avot means chapters of the fathers. It is a book of sayings.

check.q: What did Joshua ben Perachyah say to get?
check.why: His saying tells a learner to find a teacher and a friend to study with.

check.q: Where is Pirkei Avot found?
check.why: Pirkei Avot is a short book inside the Mishnah.

lessons.title: Two Houses That Argued
lessons.mainIdea: The students of Hillel and Shammai disagreed a lot, and still stayed friends.
reading: Hillel and Shammai were two rabbis. They lived about 2,000 years ago. Their students kept arguing after them. The Talmud calls the students two houses. The House of Hillel and the House of Shammai.
The two houses disagreed about many rules. They argued about food, holidays and weddings. The Talmud says they argued about some rules for three years.
But the Mishnah tells us something else. The two houses still married each other's children. They argued hard. They stayed one people. Jewish tradition remembers that.

words.d: the students who followed Hillel's way of reading the rules
the students who followed Shammai's way of reading the rules

look.title: Still One Family
look.text: The Mishnah says the House of Shammai and the House of Hillel disagreed about some marriage rules. Even so, the men of one house married women from the other house.
look.cite: Mishnah Yevamot 1:4, retold in simple words
look.prompt: The two houses disagreed. What does marrying each other's children show about them?

check.q: Who were the House of Hillel?
check.why: The House of Hillel means the students who followed Hillel's way.

check.q: What did the two houses still do?
check.why: The Mishnah says the two houses still married each other's children.

check.q: How long did the Talmud say one argument lasted?
check.why: The Talmud says the houses argued about some rules for three years.

lessons.title: Both Sides Can Be Right
lessons.mainIdea: The Talmud says both houses spoke words of the living God, and the rule follows Hillel.
reading: The Talmud tells a story about the long argument. After three years, a voice came from heaven. The voice spoke about both houses. It said: these and those are words of the living God.
Then the voice said the rule follows the House of Hillel. Why? The Talmud says Hillel's students were gentle. They taught Shammai's side first. Then they taught their own.
Jewish tradition reads this story in many ways. One reading is simple. You can lose an argument and still have said something true. And being kind helps you win.

words.d: what the Talmud's story calls both sides of the argument between the two houses

look.title: The Long Argument
rows: Sides called words of the living God
look.cite: Babylonian Talmud, Eruvin 13b, retold in simple words
look.prompt: Two sides were called true. Only one side became the rule. How can both things be so?

check.q: What did the voice call both sides?
check.why: The Talmud's story says these and those are words of the living God.

check.q: Why does the Talmud say the rule follows Hillel?
choices: His students were gentle and taught the other side first
check.why: The Talmud says Hillel's students were gentle and taught Shammai's view before their own.

check.q: In which tractate is this story found?
check.why: The story of the voice and the two houses is in Eruvin 13b.

sections.title: How to Be a Good Partner

lessons.title: Ask When You Are Stuck
lessons.mainIdea: Hillel said a shy person cannot learn, so a good partner asks questions.
reading: Pirkei Avot has a saying from Hillel. He said: a shy person cannot learn. And a person with a hot temper cannot teach.
What does that mean? If you are too shy to ask, you stay stuck. If you get angry fast, no one wants to ask you. So a good chavruta asks. And a good chavruta stays calm.
The rabbis liked questions. Another rabbi, Chanina, said he learned a lot from his teachers. He learned more from his friends. He learned the most from his students. Their questions taught him.

words.d: what you ask when you do not understand; the rabbis said questions are how you learn

look.title: Two Things Hillel Said
look.text: Hillel said: A shy person does not learn, and a person who gets angry easily does not teach.
look.cite: Mishnah Avot 2:5, retold in simple words; compare Charles Taylor, Sayings of the Jewish Fathers, 1877
look.prompt: Why would being shy stop you from learning? What could a partner do to help?

check.q: Who cannot learn, in Hillel's saying?
check.why: Hillel said a shy person cannot learn, because that person does not ask.

check.q: Who did Rabbi Chanina say he learned the most from?
check.why: Rabbi Chanina said he learned most from his students and their questions (Ta'anit 7a).

check.q: What should you do when you are stuck?
check.why: A good chavruta asks. The rabbis said questions are how you learn.

lessons.title: Say Why, Gently
lessons.mainIdea: A study partner is a friend who makes you think, so you say why, not just no.
reading: Sometimes your partner is wrong. What do you do? You do not just say no. You say why. You point to the page. You show the line. And you say it gently.
The Talmud tells of two partners. They were Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish. One taught a rule. The other asked many hard questions. The Talmud says that made the rule clear.
Later, Rabbi Yochanan lost his partner. Someone else came to study with him. That person only agreed. Rabbi Yochanan was sad. He missed the hard questions. A friend who makes you think is a gift.

words.d: in a soft, kind way; how a good partner says you are wrong
a rabbi in the Talmud whose hard questions helped his partner Rabbi Yochanan think

look.title: Two Ways to Say It
look.text: Partner A says: "No. You are wrong. That is dumb." Partner B says: "Hmm. I read it a different way. Look at this line. It says the lamp is by the door. Does that change it?" Both partners think the same thing. Only one of them is a good chavruta.
look.prompt: Which partner would you want? Say what Partner B did that Partner A did not.

check.q: What do you do when your partner is wrong?
check.why: A good partner says why, points to the page, and stays gentle.

check.q: Who was Rabbi Yochanan's study partner?
check.why: Resh Lakish was Rabbi Yochanan's partner. His questions made the rules clear.

check.q: Why was Rabbi Yochanan sad with his new partner?
check.why: The Talmud says the new partner only agreed, and Rabbi Yochanan missed the hard questions.

review.why: A chavruta is a study partner. The word comes from a word for friend.

review.q: How is the Talmud usually studied?
review.why: Jewish tradition studies the Talmud in pairs, out loud, with questions.

review.q: Which two houses argued for three years?
review.why: The Talmud says the House of Hillel and the House of Shammai argued for three years (Eruvin 13b).

review.q: What did the Mishnah say the two houses still did?
review.why: Mishnah Yevamot 1:4 says the houses still married each other's children.

review.q: Hillel said a shy person cannot do what?
review.why: Hillel's saying in Pirkei Avot is that a shy person cannot learn.

review.q: What did Resh Lakish give his partner?
review.why: The Talmud says Resh Lakish asked many hard questions, and that made the rules clear.

chapters.title: Kindness Rules from the Rabbis
chapters.bigQuestion: What kindness rules did the rabbis write down, and who does each rule help?

story.title: The Lost Mitten
story.kicker: One red mitten in the snow, and a whole class decides what to do about it.
paragraphs: It is a cold day in Chicago. Recess is over. Jada finds a red mitten in the snow. It is not hers. It has a small yellow star on it. She holds it up. "Whose is this?" Nobody answers.
Back inside, the class talks about it. Ben says, "Finders keepers." Jada shakes her head. "Somebody's hand is cold right now." Mr. Ortiz asks, "So what should a finder do?"

The class makes a rule. A finder does not keep it. A finder puts it in the Lost Box. A finder says what it looks like, but not everything. The owner has to say the secret part. "Mine has a yellow star," someone would say.

Mr. Ortiz smiles. "You just did what the rabbis did," he says. "They asked the same question. They wrote their answer in a book called the Talmud. This week, we will read some of their kindness rules."
story.think: Why did the class say the owner has to tell the secret part of the mitten? What would go wrong without that rule?

lessons.title: Visiting the Sick
lessons.mainIdea: The rabbis said visiting a sick person is a mitzvah, and it makes them feel better.
reading: A rule in the Torah is called a *mitzvah*. The rabbis found many mitzvot about being kind. One is visiting someone who is sick. The Hebrew name is bikkur cholim.
The Talmud tells why. It says God visited Abraham when he was hurting. The rabbis read that as a lesson. If God visits the sick, people should too.
The Talmud also says a visit helps. One rabbi said a visit takes away a bit of the sickness. A sick person is not alone. That feels better.

words.d: a rule in the Torah; the rabbis also use it for a good deed; more than one is mitzvot
visiting the sick, a mitzvah the rabbis talked about in the Talmud

look.title: Why Visit?
look.text: The Talmud says: Just as God visited the sick, when God came to Abraham after he was hurt, so you should visit the sick.
look.cite: Babylonian Talmud, Sotah 14a, retold in simple words; the verse is Genesis 18:1
look.prompt: The rabbis read a story about Abraham as a rule for everyone. What is the rule?

check.q: What is a mitzvah?
check.why: A mitzvah is a rule in the Torah. The rabbis also use the word for a good deed.

check.q: Who did the Talmud say God visited?
check.why: The Talmud (Sotah 14a) says God visited Abraham after he was hurt.

check.q: What does bikkur cholim mean?
check.why: Bikkur cholim is the Hebrew name for visiting the sick.

lessons.title: Welcoming a Guest
lessons.mainIdea: The Torah says Abraham ran to feed three strangers, and the rabbis made that a rule.
reading: The Torah tells a story about Abraham. He sat by his tent on a hot day. Three strangers walked by. Abraham ran to them. He asked them to rest. He brought water and bread. He served a big meal.
The rabbis loved this story. They said welcoming a *guest* is a great mitzvah. The Hebrew name is hachnasat orchim. That means bringing in guests.
The Talmud says something big about it. It says welcoming guests is even greater than greeting God. Why? Because Abraham left God's presence to run to the strangers. The rabbis read that as a lesson.

words.d: a person who comes to your home or table; the rabbis said to welcome guests warmly
bringing in guests; the rabbis' name for the mitzvah of welcoming people

look.title: Abraham's Meal
rows: Measures of flour for the bread
look.prompt: Abraham made a very big meal for three people. What does that tell you about how he treated guests?

check.q: What did Abraham do when he saw the strangers?
check.why: Genesis 18 says Abraham ran to meet the strangers and fed them.

check.q: What does hachnasat orchim mean?
check.why: Hachnasat orchim means bringing in guests. It is the mitzvah of welcoming.

check.q: Which book tells the story of Abraham's guests?
check.why: The story is in Genesis 18, the first book of the Torah.

lessons.title: Honoring Parents
lessons.mainIdea: The Torah says honor your father and mother, and the Talmud tells how.
reading: One of the Ten Commandments is about parents. The Torah says: honor your father and your mother. The rabbis asked, what does *honor* mean? What do you actually do?
The Talmud gives a list. You help them eat. You help them dress. You help them get around. You speak to them with respect.

The Talmud also tells a story. A man named Dama had a rare stone to sell. Buyers offered a lot of money. But the key was under his sleeping father's pillow. Dama would not wake him. He lost the sale. The rabbis said that is honor.

words.d: to treat someone with respect and care; the Torah tells children to honor their parents

look.title: The Commandment
look.text: Honour thy father and thy mother, that thy days may be long upon the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee.
look.prompt: This is old English. Say it in your own words. What does it tell a child to do?

check.q: Which commandment is this lesson about?
check.why: The lesson is about the commandment to honor your father and mother (Exodus 20:12).

check.q: Why did Dama lose the sale?
choices: He would not wake his father
check.why: The Talmud (Kiddushin 31a) says the key was under his sleeping father's pillow, and Dama would not wake him.

check.q: What is one way the Talmud says to honor parents?
check.why: The Talmud lists helping parents eat, dress and get around as ways to honor them.

lessons.title: Do Not Shame Anyone
lessons.mainIdea: The rabbis said shaming someone in front of others hurts as much as a wound.
reading: Words can hurt. The rabbis knew this. The Talmud says do not *shame* a person in front of others. Shame is when someone feels small and everyone sees.
The Talmud says a shamed person's face turns white. The rabbis compared that to a wound. They said it is a very serious thing to do.
The rabbis even said this. It is better to be thrown into a fire than to shame someone in public. That is a strong way to talk. It shows how much the rule mattered to them.

words.d: to make someone feel small in front of others; the rabbis said never to do it

look.title: At the Lunch Table
look.text: Look at the lunch table. Sam spills milk on his shirt. Everyone is watching. One kid points and laughs loudly. Another kid hands Sam a napkin and starts talking about the game at recess. Sam's face was red. Now it is not.
look.prompt: Which kid followed the rabbis' rule about shame? What did that kid do to help?

check.q: What does the Talmud say not to do in public?
check.why: The Talmud (Bava Metzia 58b) says not to shame a person in front of others.

check.q: What did the rabbis compare shaming to?
check.why: The rabbis said a shamed person's face goes white, like a wound.

check.q: What is shame?
check.why: Shame is feeling small in front of others. The rabbis said never to cause it.

lessons.title: Returning Lost Things
lessons.mainIdea: The Torah says bring a lost thing back, and the Mishnah says how to find the owner.
reading: The Torah has a rule about lost things. If you see your neighbor's lost animal, do not walk past. Bring it back. The rabbis read this for all lost things.
The Mishnah asks how. A finder says out loud what was found. The owner gives a *sign*. A sign is a secret detail only the owner knows. If the sign matches, the thing goes home.
That is like the class rule about the mitten. The finder says: a red mitten. The owner says: with a yellow star. The rabbis wrote this in a tractate called Bava Metzia.

words.d: a secret detail that shows a lost thing is really yours
a tractate of the Talmud about lost things, buying, selling and being fair; the name means the middle gate

look.title: Do Not Walk Past
look.text: The Torah says: If you see your neighbor's ox or sheep wandering, do not hide and pretend you did not see. Bring it back to your neighbor.
look.cite: Deuteronomy 22:1, retold in simple words from the Jewish Publication Society translation, 1917
look.prompt: The verse talks about an ox and a sheep. What else could the rule be about today?

check.q: What is a sign, in the Mishnah's rule?
choices: A secret detail only the owner knows
check.why: A sign is a secret detail. The owner gives it, and it shows the thing is theirs.

check.q: What does the Torah say to do with a lost animal?
check.why: Deuteronomy 22:1 says not to hide from it, but to bring it back.

check.q: Which tractate has the rules for lost things?
check.why: Bava Metzia, the middle gate, has the rules about lost things.

lessons.title: A Share for Those in Need
lessons.mainIdea: Tzedakah is giving a share to people who need it, and the rabbis said everyone gives.
reading: The Torah tells farmers to leave the corners of a field. Poor people come and take what grows there. The rabbis made a bigger rule from this. It is called *tzedakah*.
Tzedakah means giving a share to people who need it. The word comes from a word for fair. The rabbis said it is not extra. It is what is fair.
The Talmud says even a poor person gives tzedakah. Everyone has something to give. Later, a rabbi named Maimonides made a ladder of giving. The best step is helping someone earn their own.

words.d: giving a share to people who need it; the word comes from a word for fair

look.title: The Ladder of Giving
rows: Steps on Maimonides's ladder of giving
Best step: helping someone earn their own
Middle step: giving without knowing who gets it
Lowest step: giving with a frown
look.cite: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Gifts to the Poor 10:7–14 (c. 1180), retold in simple words
look.prompt: Why do you think helping someone earn their own is the best step?

check.q: What does tzedakah mean?
choices: Giving a share to people in need
check.why: Tzedakah is giving a share to people who need it. The word comes from a word for fair.

check.q: Who did the Talmud say gives tzedakah?
check.why: The Talmud (Gittin 7b) says even a poor person gives tzedakah.

check.q: What did Maimonides make?
check.why: Maimonides listed eight steps of giving, from lowest to best.

lessons.title: Feed the Animals First
lessons.mainIdea: The Talmud says to feed your animals before you eat, because they cannot ask.
reading: Here is a small rule with a big heart. The Talmud says feed your *animals* before you sit down to eat. Your dog cannot open the fridge. Your goat cannot ask for hay.
The rabbis found this in a verse. The Torah says God gives grass for your cattle, and then you will eat. The grass comes first in the verse. The rabbis read that order as a rule.

Now you have read seven kindness rules. Each one helps someone. The sick person. The guest. The parent. The shamed person. The owner. The person in need. The hungry animal. The rabbis wrote rules to help them.

words.d: creatures in your care; the Talmud says to feed them before you eat

look.title: Who Does Each Rule Help?
look.text: Look at a table with seven cards. One card says Visit. One says Welcome. One says Honor. One says Do not shame. One says Bring it back. One says Give a share. One says Feed the animals. Under each card is a picture of a person or an animal.
look.prompt: Pick three cards. Say who each rule helps, and how you could do it this week.

check.q: When does the Talmud say to feed your animals?
check.why: The Talmud (Berakhot 40a) says to feed your animals before you sit down to eat.

check.q: Where did the rabbis find this rule?
choices: In a verse of the Torah
check.why: The rabbis read Deuteronomy 11:15, where grass for cattle comes before eating.

check.q: Who does the rule about lost things help?
check.why: Bringing a lost thing back helps the owner who lost it.

review.why: A mitzvah is a rule in the Torah. The rabbis also use it for a good deed.

review.q: Who ran to feed three strangers?
review.why: Genesis 18 says Abraham ran to the strangers and served them a meal.

review.q: What did Dama refuse to do?
review.why: The Talmud says Dama lost a sale rather than wake his father.

review.q: What does the owner give to get a lost thing back?
review.why: The Mishnah says the owner gives a sign, a secret detail only the owner knows.

review.q: What does the word tzedakah come from?
review.why: Tzedakah comes from a word for fair. The rabbis said giving is what is fair.

review.q: What did the rabbis compare shaming someone to?
review.why: The Talmud says a shamed face goes white, like a wound.
